extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of narratology, literary critics, and advanced creative writers studying narrative voice and levels
extracted.subtask_description: Analytic framework for identifying and classifying narrative instances, levels (extradiegetic/diegetic/metadiegetic), modes (oral/written/inward), metalepsis, and relations among embedded narratives in literary texts. Useful for close reading and theorizing how narration functions and affects diegetic events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrative level classification (extradiegetic/diegetic/metadiegetic)
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish narrative levels: extradiegetic (narrating outside the story), diegetic (narrating within the story), and metadiegetic (second-degree narrative). Do not confuse narrative level with real historical existence (e.g., Paris vs Balbec).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these labels to locate narrating instances in the text; note that extradiegetic narrating may refer to real or fictive places equally. Example: the extradiegetic narrator who addresses a public vs intradiegetic narrators embedded in the story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extradiegetic narrator vs author-narrator / public address
rubrics_metrics.description: Extradiegetic narrating is not necessarily handled as a literary work with its protagonist as an author-narrator in a position to address a public; formats like diary or epistolary novels often do not 'aim at' a public and function as 'edited' documents rather than authorial addresses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check whether the narrating instance presents itself as an author addressing readers (editorial 'we', addresses to the reader) or as a private document (diary, letter). Examples: Renoncourt vs diaries/epistolary monodies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Medium/form of narrating (written, oral, interior speech, stream-of-consciousness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Narration can be written, oral, interior monologue, or a 'stream of consciousness'—the medium affects formal determinability of the narrating instance (immediate speech precludes formal determination).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify whether the narration claims to be spoken, written, or mysteriously transcribed (e.g., interior monologue 'transcribed' by another). This affects how explicitly the narrating instance can be located or described.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forms of intradiegetic (embedded) narrating
rubrics_metrics.description: Embedded narratives (intradiegesis) may be oral or written, fictional works within works, inward narratives (dreams, recollections), or nonverbal representations converted into narrative by description or report.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify embedded narratives by their form: written memoirs, discovered novellas, dream narratives, or iconographic documents described within the diegesis (examples: the Curious Impertinent in Don Quixote; Adrienne's song/memory in Sylvie).

rubrics_metrics.name: Type I: Metadiegetic relationship — direct causality / explanatory function
rubrics_metrics.description: A metadiegetic narrative whose events have direct causal links to the diegetic situation, conferring on the second narrative an explanatory function (the 'this is why' model).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for embedded narratives that answer 'what events led to the present situation?' (examples: Ulysses' narrative explaining events leading to his arrival; Des Grieux). These often serve cognitive/explanatory purposes and may be pretextual for reader curiosity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Type II: Metadiegetic relationship — thematic relationship (contrast/analogy/en abyme)
rubrics_metrics.description: A metadiegetic narrative linked to the diegesis purely thematically — by contrast, analogy, or an en abyme structure — without spatio-temporal continuity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify instances where an embedded tale functions as an exemplum or mirror (contrast or analogy) for diegetic events, potentially influencing characters (e.g., Amram's story persuading Jocabel; parable/fable structures). The 'en abyme' is an extreme analogy approaching identity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Type III: Metadiegetic relationship — narrating act as diegetic function (distraction/obstruction)
rubrics_metrics.description: A case where the act of narrating itself (independently of content) serves a diegetic function such as distraction or delay.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detect narratives used instrumentally to produce diegetic effects — classic example: Scheherazade's stories that postpone death regardless of content. Assess how the communicative act functions within the diegesis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Metalepsis (narrative transgression between levels)
rubrics_metrics.description: Transitions or transgressions between narrative levels effected by intrusion (authorial or diegetic), producing effects of strangeness, comedy, or the fantastic — e.g., author's metalepsis or inverse metalepsis where diegetic events affect the narrating world.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify intrusions of extradiegetic figures into diegetic worlds (or vice versa) and classify their tonal effect (comic in Sterne/Diderot; uncanny or fantastic in others). Example: Cortazar's inverse metalepsis or Virgil 'has Dido die' as author's metalepsis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pseudo-diegetic (reduced metadiegetic) narration
rubrics_metrics.description: Narration originally of metadiegetic origin that is immediately 'brought to' the first level and appropriated by the primary narrator, effectively reducing or eliding the intermediary narrative level (pseudo-diegetic).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detect when an embedded narrative's intermediary narrator is neutralized and the extradiegetic narrator retells the material as part of his own narrative. Signs can be subtle; one indicator is the absence of expected markers (e.g., shift from 'he' to 'I'). Theaetetus exemplifies explicit reduction; Proust's Recherche frequently practices pseudo-diegetic appropriation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Markers of narrative-level transitions
rubrics_metrics.description: In literature, level changes are often signalled by shifts in grammatical person, typographic conventions (italics, bold), or explicit editorial cues; in film, by visual/sound devices (blur, slow motion, voice-off, color changes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing a text, look for these cues to disambiguate whether a passage is metadiegetic or diegetic; absence of markers can make metadiegetic origin imperceptible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrator presence vs grammatical person: heterodiegetic vs homodiegetic
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not equate grammatical 'first-person' with narrator presence in the story. Distinguish heterodiegetic narrators (absent from the story they tell) from homodiegetic narrators (present as characters in their story).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify narratives by whether the narrator is a character of the narrated story (homodiegetic, e.g., Gil Blas, Wuthering Heights) or outside it (heterodiegetic, e.g., Homer, Flaubert). Recognize editorial plural forms that complicate simple 'first/third person' labels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Source/origin of analepses (memory vs report) and implications
rubrics_metrics.description: Analepses (retrospections) may originate in the narrator's memory (inward narrative) or in reports made to the narrator by third persons; origin affects whether the return is pseudo-diegetic and how the narrator incorporates the material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine whether a flashback is presented as personally remembered (which the narrator may then take direct control of) or as information mediated by another character; this influences claims of narrative monopoly and authorial appropriation (examples from Proust: Balbec memories vs reports about Swann).

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrative control, unity of instance, and egocentrism
rubrics_metrics.description: A narrative choice concerns whether the narrator preserves unity and monopoly of narrating instance (narrative egocentrism) by appropriating embedded narratives rather than letting other characters 'take the floor.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the narrator insists on telling all accounts (Proust's Marcel takes control of Swann's tale) versus allowing embedded narrators autonomy; this affects the perceived unity of instance and narrative authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: 'Chinese-box' (nested) narrative / narrative splitting
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of nested narratives (stories within stories, multiple hypostases) creates a domino or 'Chinese-box' structure and can serve distancing or archaic effects; e.g., Jean Santeuil's split narrating instance and discovered-manuscript framing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify nested frames and whether they are oral/written, and note their rhetorical effects (distancing, historicizing, or timidity at direct novelistic writing). Consider whether the author later reduces such nesting (as Proust does in Recherche).

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrative as performative instrument (creating or determining events)
rubrics_metrics.description: Narrative can be performative: telling a story can bring events into being or set in motion diegetic consequences (e.g., the oracle in Oedipus; Swann's recounted love shaping Marcel's future imaginings).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze instances where a recounted narrative functions causally or motivationally in the diegesis, not merely representationally. Consider the ethical/ontological implication that narrative can 'give life' or 'take life.'
